Section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 specifies what types of property or interests may or may not be transferred. It states that property of any kind may be transferred except in certain cases. These exceptions include: (a) mere chances of inheritance or legacy, (b) a mere right of re-entry for breach of a condition subsequent, (c) easements without the dominant heritage, (d) interests restricted to personal enjoyment, (e) rights to future maintenance, (f) public offices or salaries of public officers, (g) stipends and political pensions, (h) transfers that are contrary to the nature of the interest, unlawful object or consideration, or to a legally disqualified person, and (i) certain tenants, farmers, or lessees who are restricted by law in their capacity. The section also clarifies that a tenant with an untransferable right of occupancy, a farmer with default in revenue payment, or a lessee under a Court of Wards cannot assign their interest in such capacity.

Section 7 of the Contract Act, 1872 requires that acceptance of a proposal must be absolute and unqualified. It also states that acceptance must be expressed in a usual and reasonable manner, unless the proposal specifies otherwise. If the proposal prescribes a manner of acceptance and the acceptance is not made in that manner, the proposer may, within a reasonable time, insist on acceptance in the prescribed manner; if they fail to do so, they are deemed to have accepted the acceptance in the manner it was given.

The Sindh High Court dismissed the criminal acquittal appeal filed by the appellant, upholding the acquittal of Respondent No.1 by the trial court. The court held that the trial court's decision was correct, particularly in view of the admitted fact that the complainant had legally handed over the house for renovation and that the accused had not committed theft as no physical evidence or eyewitness was available. The court also emphasized that the scope of an acquittal appeal is narrow and that each case must be decided on its own merits, and therefore, no interference was warranted.

The final outcome in AHSAN v. The State (Cr.Acq.A. 124/2019) was that the appeal against the acquittal was dismissed in limine. The Sindh High Court held that the trial court's acquittal of the private respondent was not arbitrary or perverse, and that the prosecution had not established any glaring errors of fact or law. The court emphasized that interference with an acquittal is rare and requires a showing of perversity, arbitrariness, or grave factual infirmities, none of which were present in this case.

The law on transfer of actionable claim applicable to the date of 11 September 2020 is governed by Section 130, 131, 132, and 136 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Under Section 130, the transfer of an actionable claim is effective upon execution of a written instrument signed by the transferor or his duly authorized agent, and the transferee acquires all rights and remedies of the transferor, including the right to sue in his own name, without needing the transferor's consent. Section 131 requires that notice of transfer must be in writing and signed by the transferor or his agent, or by the transferee or his agent, stating the name and address of the transferee. Section 132 imposes liability on the transferee, who takes the claim subject to all liabilities and equities that the transferor had at the time of transfer, including the right to set off debts. Section 136 prohibits judges, legal practitioners, or officers connected with courts from buying or trafficking in actionable claims. These provisions were in force on 11 September 2020 as no amendments to the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, specifically affecting actionable claims, were introduced after the date of the Act's enactment and are not superseded by any subsequent legislation as of that date.

These implied contracts attach to the mortgagee's interest and can be enforced by any person who holds that interest. Additionally, subsection 65A provides that a mortgagor may lease the mortgaged property while in lawful possession, subject to certain conditions: the lease must be in the ordinary course of management, reserve the best rent reasonably obtainable, not include a premium or advance rent, not contain a covenant for renewal, and take effect within six months of execution. For building leases, the lease duration cannot exceed three years and must include a rent payment covenant and a re-entry condition. These provisions apply only if not expressly contradicted in the mortgage deed, and may be varied or extended by the mortgage deed, with such variations operating as if they were originally included.
